cards.explanation: The answer is saddled donkeys loaded with food and wine. Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, brought a pair of saddled donkeys to meet David. They carried two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits and a skin of wine. Those donkeys put in a longer shift than I do on cookie Saturday.

The word is king. David asks Ziba why he has all this, and Ziba says, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat…” He adds that the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness. Donkeys for riding, food for eating, wine for the worn out. I can't even explain my own cookie budget that clearly, friends.

The answer is True. David asks where Mephibosheth is, and Ziba answers that he is staying in Jerusalem. Then Ziba reports that Mephibosheth has said, “Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.” Notice, friends, that this is what Ziba says Mephibosheth said.

The answer is that David gives Ziba all his master's property. David tells Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” That's a big gift to hand out on a dusty road after one short conversation. Ziba answers by bowing and asking, “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king!”

The answer is that Shimei yells curses and throws stones. Shimei son of Gera, a man from the family of the house of Saul, kept yelling out curses as he came closer. He threw stones at David and at all the king's servants. The troops and mighty men were right there on David's right and left, and he threw anyway.

The word is LORD. Shimei yells, “The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned…” He adds that the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of David's son Absalom. Those are Shimei's words, spoken while he's yelling and throwing stones. Hold onto that, friends, because David has an answer coming.

The answer is that Abishai asks to go over and cut off Shimei's head. Abishai son of Zeruiah, one of David's men, says, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head!” It's a heavy moment, and I think Abishai was ready to act right then. Next comes David's answer.

The answer is that the LORD may have told Shimei to curse him. David says to Abishai, “If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’…” He doesn't answer Shimei with a fight. He says "if," and leaves room for the LORD to be behind it. That's a lot to say with stones flying at him.

The answer is False. David does not give Abishai the go-ahead. He says, “Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.” That's David turning down Abishai's request, and he tells both Abishai and all his servants to let Shimei be.

The word is good. David says, “Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.” Notice the "perhaps," friends. David isn't demanding anything. He's hoping, with stones still flying.

The answer is False. The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted. And there he refreshed himself. After a road like that, one with curses, stones and dust, I'd need a long sit-down too, probably with my mustache hanging.
